section.h2: Frequently Asked Questions About Peritoneal Metastasis in Gastric Cancer: HIPEC and PIPAC in China
section.intro: These FAQs explain how HIPEC and PIPAC are used for peritoneal spread of gastric cancer, who may be suitable, and how international patients can explore these options at centers in China.

groups.title: Understanding Peritoneal Metastasis, HIPEC, and PIPAC

items.q: What is peritoneal metastasis in gastric cancer?
items.a: Peritoneal metastasis means gastric cancer cells have spread to the peritoneum, the thin membrane lining the abdominal cavity and organs. It is a common pattern of advanced gastric cancer and may cause abdominal fluid buildup (ascites), bloating, pain, or bowel problems. Because standard imaging can miss small deposits, diagnosis often needs laparoscopy or cytology. Treatment depends on cancer type, extent of spread, previous therapy, and specialist review.

items.q: What is HIPEC for gastric cancer?
items.a: HIPEC (Hyperthermic Intraperitoneal Chemotherapy) is heated chemotherapy delivered directly into the abdomen during surgery. After a surgeon removes visible tumor deposits (cytoreductive surgery), warmed chemotherapy is circulated inside the abdominal cavity to target remaining microscopic cancer cells. The heat may improve drug penetration. HIPEC is a complex procedure considered only for carefully selected patients with limited peritoneal spread, and suitability should be decided by an experienced oncology and surgical team.

items.q: What is PIPAC and how is it different from HIPEC?
items.a: PIPAC (Pressurized Intraperitoneal Aerosol Chemotherapy) delivers chemotherapy as a fine aerosol spray into the abdomen through keyhole (laparoscopic) surgery. Unlike HIPEC, PIPAC does not require major tumor-removal surgery and is usually repeated every few weeks. It aims to control disease and symptoms in patients with more extensive peritoneal spread who are not candidates for HIPEC. Both are specialized options, and choice depends on disease extent and overall health.

items.q: How do doctors confirm peritoneal spread before HIPEC or PIPAC?
items.a: Peritoneal spread is usually confirmed with diagnostic laparoscopy, where a camera inspects the abdominal cavity and washings are checked for cancer cells. CT or MRI scans, PET imaging, and analysis of ascites fluid may support the assessment, but small deposits can be missed on scans alone. Doctors also grade the extent using a peritoneal cancer index. Accurate staging guides whether HIPEC, PIPAC, or systemic therapy is most appropriate for each patient.

items.q: Who is eligible for HIPEC in gastric cancer?
items.a: HIPEC may be considered for selected patients with limited peritoneal spread whose main tumor and visible deposits can be surgically removed. Good candidates usually have reasonable general fitness, controlled disease elsewhere, and adequate organ function. Patients with widespread peritoneal disease, distant organ metastases, or poor performance status are often not suitable. Final eligibility depends on cancer stage, peritoneal cancer index, previous treatment, and detailed assessment by the surgical oncology team.

items.q: Who may be suitable for PIPAC?
items.a: PIPAC may be suitable for selected patients with peritoneal spread that is too extensive for complete surgical removal, or who need disease and symptom control between systemic treatments. Because it is minimally invasive and repeatable, it can sometimes be offered to patients who cannot undergo major surgery. Suitability still depends on overall health, ability to tolerate anesthesia, prior treatment, and specialist review, and it is not appropriate for everyone.

items.q: How is the HIPEC or PIPAC procedure performed?
items.a: HIPEC begins with cytoreductive surgery to remove visible tumor, followed by circulating heated chemotherapy inside the abdomen for roughly 60–90 minutes before closing. PIPAC is done through small laparoscopic incisions, spraying aerosolized chemotherapy under pressure for a short time, and is typically repeated in cycles. Both are performed under general anesthesia in specialized centers. The exact technique, drugs, and timing are decided by the treating team based on individual findings.

items.q: What are the risks and side effects of HIPEC and PIPAC?
items.a: Possible risks include bleeding, infection, bowel injury, delayed healing, kidney effects, and chemotherapy-related side effects such as low blood counts or nausea. HIPEC, being a larger operation, carries higher surgical risk and a longer recovery than PIPAC. Serious complications are uncommon in experienced centers but can occur. These procedures do not guarantee a cure, and the balance of benefits and risks should be discussed carefully with the treating oncology team.

items.q: How much do HIPEC and PIPAC cost in China?
items.a: Costs vary widely and cannot be quoted as a fixed figure. HIPEC generally costs more than PIPAC because it involves major surgery, longer hospital stay, and intensive care. Final cost depends on the hospital, diagnosis, disease extent, chemotherapy drugs used, number of PIPAC cycles, tests, complications, and length of stay. International patients should request a written estimate from the chosen center and confirm what services are included before travel.

items.q: Which hospitals in China offer HIPEC and PIPAC?
items.a: Several large cancer and university hospitals in cities such as Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, and other major centers have developed peritoneal surface malignancy programs offering HIPEC, and some also perform PIPAC. Availability, experience, and case volume differ between centers. Because these are specialized procedures, it is important to choose a hospital with an experienced surgical oncology team. A medical coordinator can help identify centers that match a patient's specific diagnosis.

items.q: Are HIPEC and PIPAC available outside China?
items.a: Yes, HIPEC is available in many countries, including specialized centers in India, parts of Europe, and the United States, while PIPAC is offered in a smaller number of centers worldwide. Availability, waiting times, drug protocols, and cost differ significantly by country. Some patients consider China for access to PIPAC programs or shorter waiting periods. The best location depends on the individual case and should be reviewed with qualified specialists.

items.q: How can international patients access HIPEC or PIPAC in China?
items.a: Access depends on hospital acceptance after medical record review, disease suitability, travel fitness, and visa approval, and none of these can be guaranteed in advance. International patients usually send recent scans, pathology, and treatment history for assessment, then receive an opinion on whether HIPEC or PIPAC may be considered. If accepted, the center helps arrange appointments and estimates. Final treatment decisions are always made by the treating medical team.

items.q: Can HIPEC or PIPAC be combined with chemotherapy or immunotherapy?
items.a: HIPEC and PIPAC are usually part of a broader plan that includes systemic chemotherapy, and in some cases targeted therapy or immunotherapy based on biomarker results. For example, systemic treatment may be given before or after these procedures to control disease throughout the body. The combination depends on cancer type, HER2 or other biomarker status, previous treatment, and overall health, and should be planned by a multidisciplinary oncology team.

items.q: Are there clinical trials for peritoneal metastasis in gastric cancer?
items.a: Yes, clinical trials are studying HIPEC, PIPAC, new drug combinations, and immunotherapy for peritoneal spread of gastric cancer in China and other countries. Trials may offer access to newer approaches but cannot guarantee benefit or enrollment. Eligibility is decided only after review of medical records and investigator assessment, and trials often have strict inclusion and exclusion criteria. A specialist can advise whether any current trial may be relevant.

items.q: Does HIPEC or PIPAC cure peritoneal metastasis?
items.a: HIPEC and PIPAC do not offer a guaranteed cure for peritoneal metastasis in gastric cancer. For carefully selected patients, HIPEC combined with complete tumor removal may improve disease control and, in some cases, survival, while PIPAC mainly aims to slow progression and ease symptoms. Outcomes depend on disease extent, response to treatment, and overall health. Realistic goals should be discussed openly with the treating oncology team before deciding.

items.q: What medical reports are needed to assess HIPEC or PIPAC eligibility?
items.a: Useful reports include recent CT or MRI scans, any PET scan, the endoscopy and biopsy pathology report, biomarker results such as HER2, prior treatment summaries, and current blood tests. Findings from a diagnostic laparoscopy, if available, are especially helpful for judging peritoneal spread. Organizing complete, up-to-date records allows specialists to give a more accurate opinion. The treating team may request additional tests before confirming whether a procedure is appropriate.

items.q: How long is the hospital stay and recovery for HIPEC and PIPAC?
items.a: Hospital stay differs between the two procedures. HIPEC often needs a stay of one to two weeks or longer, with several weeks of recovery afterward because it involves major surgery. PIPAC is minimally invasive, so patients may stay only a few days per cycle and recover more quickly. Actual timelines depend on the individual, the extent of surgery, and any complications, and should be confirmed with the treating center.

items.a: CancerFax helps patients organize medical reports, identify relevant specialists or treatment centers, estimate possible costs, and coordinate second opinions, appointments, travel, visa, and follow-up support.
